source: Ferguson (UCLA book) Optimal Stopping and Applications, ch.2 Finite Horizon Problems
finding: Defines the classical secretary problem (8 assumptions) and solves it by backward induction. Optimal rule is a threshold rule: reject the first r-1, accept the next relatively best. Stopping on a candidate at position j wins with chance j/n.
numbers: Optimal r and win prob for n=1..8: r=1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4; P=1.0,.500,.500,.458,.433,.428,.414,.410. Large n: r/n tends to 1/e = 36.8%, and win prob tends to 1/e.
quote: Pass up a proportion e^-1 = 36.8% of the applicants and then select the next candidate.
limits: Only rank information, known n, no recall, win only on the single best.
agent_relevance: A stop rule is a threshold on observed state plus a count of items seen. The optimum depends on a known horizon n.

source: Ferguson ch.2 (arbitrary monotonic utility; Chow, Moriguti, Robbins, Samuels 1964 expected-rank problem; Lindley 1961)
finding: If the goal is a low expected rank rather than the single best, the optimal rule is staged: accept lower relative ranks as the sequence goes on. Lindley (1961) introduced it; Chow et al. (1964) solved the limit.
numbers: Limit expected rank 3.8695. Cut points b(1)=.2584, b(2)=.4476, b(3)=.5640 of the sequence: wait 25.8% then take rank 1; after 44.8% take rank 1 or 2; after 56.4% take rank 1 to 3.
limits: Rank-only payoffs; asymptotic results. The 37% rule is specific to a win-only-on-best payoff.
agent_relevance: With graded payoffs the stop bar should relax in stages as the budget is used up (G11 spending rule), not stay fixed.

source: Ferguson ch.3 Existence of Optimal Rules: principle of optimality and the optimality equation
finding: Gives the dynamic-programming optimality equation: V_n = max(Y_n, E[V_{n+1} given F_n]). Stop when the reward for stopping now is at least the expected value of continuing. Follows Chow and Robbins (1963) regular stopping rules.
numbers: Theorem 2 (optimality equation) holds under condition A1 alone. A1 plus A2 give existence of an optimal rule.
limits: The author warns the principle-of-optimality rule may be dangerous when integrability conditions fail.
agent_relevance: Core form of the S6 stop rule: compare value of stopping now with expected value of one more step.

source: Ferguson ch.4 Markov models: selling an asset with and without recall (house selling)
finding: With iid offers and cost c per look, the optimal rule is: stop at the first offer at or above a fixed reservation value V*, where V* solves E(X-V*)+ = c. Recall does not help. The problem repeats in time, so the bar is constant.
numbers: N* = min{n : X_n >= V*}; V* = E max{X1,V*} - c; unique solution for any c>0. Worked example for U(0,1).
limits: Needs iid offers, known distribution F, finite second moment.
agent_relevance: For repeated attempts with iid quality and fixed cost per attempt, the stop rule is a constant bar; the bar falls as cost per attempt rises.

source: Ferguson ch.4.5 Testing simple hypotheses; Wald sequential probability ratio test as optimal stopping
finding: Bayes-optimal sampling between two simple hypotheses, cost c per observation: the value function is concave in the posterior, so the optimal rule is two-sided. Stop when the posterior is below a or above b. This is Wald's SPRT.
numbers: N* = min{n>=0: posterior <= a or >= b}, equal to a likelihood ratio between two preset bounds. Finding a and b usually needs approximation (Wald; Siegmund 1985).
limits: Two simple hypotheses, iid data, known likelihoods.
agent_relevance: A stop rule for choosing between answers should be evidence-based (two bounds on accumulated evidence), not a fixed count. See OptPO.

source: Ferguson ch.5 Monotone stopping rule problems: k-stage look-ahead rules
finding: One-stage look-ahead (myopic) rule: stop if the reward for stopping now beats the expected reward of stopping after one more step. It is optimal in monotone problems. Two- and three-stage look-ahead are often quite good. Biesterfeld (1996) one-time look-ahead.
numbers: In the example given, the one-time look-ahead did not improve on the one-stage rule.
quote: The one-stage look-ahead rule, sometimes called the myopic rule, is reasonably good
limits: Optimal only under the monotone condition; can stop too soon when later gains are not monotone.
agent_relevance: A cheap myopic test (value of one more attempt versus its cost) is provably optimal in monotone settings. Fits a code-computed S6 trigger.

source: Ferguson ch.2 history notes: Googol, Cayley (1875), Cayley-Moser
finding: Same problem appears as the marriage problem and as Googol (largest of unknown numbers). Cayley (1875) posed a lottery-selling problem solved by backward induction; Moser recast it as a finite-horizon house-selling problem.
numbers: Googol with no distribution information: Berezovskiy and Gnedin (1984).
limits: Textbook summary; the original papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Backward induction for stopping is over 150 years old; an agent needs no new mathematics.

source: Wikipedia: Secretary problem (history and variants)
finding: History: Flood 1949 and 1958 fiancee problem; Gardner's Feb 1960 Scientific American column was the first publication; Fox and Marnie 1958 game of googol; Gilbert and Mosteller (1966) extended it. Gives the exact table for n=1..10.
numbers: P(best): n=3 .500, n=4 .458, n=5 .433, n=8 .410, n=10 .399; limit 1/e = .368. Bruss (1984) 1/e-law: success at least 1/e even if n is unknown. Cardinal payoff with uniform values: threshold near sqrt(n). Second best, one try: tends to 1/4. Top-k with k tries: tends to 1/(ek).
limits: Secondary source.
agent_relevance: The unknown-horizon guarantee suggests a stop rule that does not need to know the number of attempts.

source: Wikipedia: Secretary problem, experimental section (Seale and Rapoport 1997; Bearden et al. 2006; Palley and Kremer 2014)
finding: States that experimental psychologists and economists found people tend to stop searching too soon. No numbers on the page.
limits: Page marks this section as single-sourced. Direct check of Seale and Rapoport 1997 failed (paywalled).
agent_relevance: Humans under-search in the rank-only version; an LLM agent may show the same early-stop bias and needs its own test.

source: Wikipedia: Optimal stopping
finding: Optimal stopping can often be written as a Bellman equation and solved by dynamic programming. The martingale approach centres on the Snell envelope; the Markov approach gives free-boundary (Stefan) problems. House selling payoff y_n = X_n - n k.
numbers: Refs named: Chow, Robbins and Siegmund (1971); Peskir and Shiryaev (2006); Ferguson (2007); MacQueen and Miller (1960).
limits: No numeric examples on the page.
agent_relevance: Frames the subfield: define state, reward-if-stop, cost-of-continue, then solve backward.

source: Bearden (2006) A new secretary problem with rank-based selection and cardinal payoffs, J. Math. Psychology 50:58-59
finding: Changes the payoff: n iid uniform[0,1] values; the decision maker learns only whether each is best so far; payoff is the realised value. Proves the optimal policy skips the first sqrt(n)-1 applicants, then takes the next running maximum.
numbers: Optimal skip is sqrt(n)-1, against n/e for the win-only-on-best payoff.
quote: optimal policy dictates skipping the first sqrt(n)-1 applicants
limits: Uniform values, no recall, one choice. Short comment; the experiments are in a separate paper (Bearden, Rapoport, Murphy 2006).
agent_relevance: With graded payoffs the exploration phase is much shorter than 37%. Match the stopping rule to how the task is scored.

source: Goldstein, McAfee, Suri and Wright (2020) Learning When to Stop Searching, Management Science (preprint, names blinded)
finding: Online repeated secretary game showing values (not ranks), no information about the distribution. 6,537 players, 48,336 games. Players improve fast and approach the optimal win rate within a few games. Contradicts earlier work that found no learning.
numbers: Design 2x3: 7 or 15 boxes by low, medium, high distribution. Known-distribution optimum 62.2% (7 boxes), just under 60% (15). Classic unknown-distribution optimum .41 (7), .39 (15). Players reach the classic optimum by about game 2, then gain 10 to 15 points beyond it. 49.6% played 5+ games, 23.2% 9+, 9.3% 16+. Arm sizes in 7-box: 1145, 1082, 1103.
quote: In contrast to prior investigations that find no evidence for learning in the classical scenario, in the repeated setting we observe substantial learning
limits: No money incentive; web volunteers; win or lose feedback only. The high distribution was hardest because players stopped before the max more often. Restricting to players with 7+ games gave the same curves (not a selection effect).
agent_relevance: Experience with the value distribution lets a stopper beat the 1/e rule. An agent that logs past attempt scores could learn its own stop thresholds.

source: Goldstein et al. (2020) critical percentile table (known distribution)
finding: Full-information optimal rule gives a critical percentile for each number of boxes left: stop if the current value's percentile exceeds it. The cutoff rises as more boxes remain.
limits: Needs the true distribution; only percentiles matter, not the shape.
agent_relevance: The stop bar should depend on remaining budget: more attempts left, higher bar.

source: Goldstein et al. (2020) learning-percentiles (LP) agent and error analysis
finding: An idealised agent re-estimates percentiles within each game and applies the optimal critical values. It matches the classic optimum in game 1 and reaches the theoretical maximum within seven games. Both agent and humans more often stop before the maximum than after it.
numbers: LP agent hits the theoretical maxima in 7 or fewer games. Human stop-too-soon rate was higher in the high-distribution condition.
limits: Idealised agent has perfect memory and makes no mistakes.
agent_relevance: Early stopping is the dominant error, matching the human under-search finding.

source: Goldstein et al. (2020) Bayesian comparison of stopping models
finding: Cross-validated Bayes factors: Multiple Threshold model best, Two Threshold next, Viable-k worst. Behaviour is best described by threshold rules, a class containing the optimal strategy; fitted thresholds are close to optimal after few games.
numbers: Models: Multiple Threshold, Single Threshold, Two Threshold, Viable k. Ranking read from text: Multiple Threshold first, Two Threshold second, Viable k last.
limits: Ranking read from text; no single effect size recorded.
agent_relevance: Value-threshold rules describe good stoppers better than skip-then-take rules.

source: Goldstein et al. (2020) review of earlier null results on learning
finding: Campbell and Lee (2006) found no learning even with enriched feedback and money; Lee (2006) and Guan and Lee (2017) none in full information; Seale and Rapoport (1997) none in ranks-only. Rapoport and Tversky (1970): 7 people saw 15,600 draws. Kahan et al. (1967): groups of 22 saw up to 200 numbers.
numbers: Lee-line studies used 5 to 50 candidates and 40 to 120 plays per person.
quote: there is no evidence people learn to perform better in any condition
limits: Second-hand summary inside one paper; the original papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: The null-learning studies told people the distribution. Learning appears when the distribution must be inferred from experience.

source: Seale and Rapoport (1997) Sequential decision making with relative ranks: an experimental investigation of the secretary problem, OBHDP 69:221-236
finding: Founding human experiment on the classical rank-only secretary problem. Per secondary accounts (Goldstein 2020, Wikipedia), people stop earlier than the optimal cutoff and show no learning. Full text paywalled; only the catalogue record was opened.
numbers: Exact figures not obtained. IDEAS lists 50 citations.
limits: Not read. Treat findings as second-hand.
agent_relevance: Marks the human early-stop baseline.

source: Lee, O'Connor and Welsh (2004) Decision-making on the full information secretary problem, CogSci 26
finding: Ten people did full-information secretary problems of length 10, 20 and 50 (20 problems each, uniform 0 to 100). Accuracy fell as the sequence got longer. Some reached near-optimal accuracy; large individual differences.
numbers: Mean accuracy 54.5% (n=10), 47.0% (n=20), 43.0% (n=50). Per-person means from 33.3% to 61.4%. Mean age 26.1; 4 men, 6 women.
quote: some people achieve near-optimal levels of accuracy, but that there are individual differences
limits: N=10; fixed order of lengths (10, then 20, then 50). Told the distribution.
agent_relevance: Even simple stopping tasks show wide person-to-person spread; do not assume one human-like rule.

source: Lee et al. (2004) heuristic models: biased optimal, threshold, cutoff (MDL comparison)
finding: Compared three stop heuristics: biased version of the optimal position-dependent threshold; single fixed threshold; cutoff (skip a proportion then take the next above the max). By Minimum Description Length, people used the biased-optimal or threshold rules, not the cutoff rule. Individuals were consistent across lengths in which heuristic they used.
numbers: Flexibility: of 1020 decision patterns for length-10 sets, heuristics can reproduce 78 (biased optimal), 60 (threshold), 9 (cutoff). Decisions predicted correctly where each rule fit: biased optimal 81%, 78%, 88% (n=10, 20, 50); threshold 74%, 78%, 79%.
limits: N=10. The cutoff heuristic is optimal for the rank-only version but a poor description when values are shown.
agent_relevance: When values are visible, a value-threshold stop rule beats skip-and-take and is also more human-like.

source: Lee et al. (2004) accuracy of heuristics across their parameter spaces
finding: The threshold heuristic can reach higher accuracy than the cutoff heuristic in the full-information task, but biased-optimal and threshold heuristics are both very sensitive to their parameter values.
numbers: Qualitative from the text; figure values not extracted.
limits: Figure values not read.
agent_relevance: Stop thresholds need calibration; a badly set bar loses a lot of accuracy.

source: Gilbert and Mosteller (1966) Recognizing the maximum of a sequence (as described by Lee et al. 2004 and Wikipedia)
finding: Gave optimal cutoffs for the rank version (limit 1/e) and optimal position-dependent thresholds and win probabilities for the full-information version (their Tables 2, 7, 8). Extended to several acceptance chances, up to four.
numbers: Rank-version limit 0.368. Table values not opened.
limits: Original not opened; known through two secondary sources.
agent_relevance: Source of exact thresholds when values are visible.

source: Kalayci, Raman and Dughmi (2025) Optimal stopping vs best-of-N for inference time optimization, arXiv 2510.01394
finding: Treats each LLM generation as opening a Pandora's Box (Weitzman 1978). A UCB-style algorithm learns the stopping threshold without knowing the reward distribution, with provable closeness to Weitzman's optimum. A Bradley-Terry transform normalises rewards across prompts.
numbers: Same quality as non-adaptive Best-of-N with 15 to 35% fewer generations on average (AlpacaFarm, HH-RLHF). Win rate over Best-of-N at equal average samples above 54% in most cost settings (cost 1e-5 to 1e-3, 100 random orderings per prompt). Saving rises from 15% to 35% as the target acceptance rate goes up from 0.75. 1,600 generation profiles in the profit test.
limits: Reward-model scores, not task correctness; chat data; main figure uses Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 with RM-Mistral-7B.
agent_relevance: A direct, tested template for the S3/S6 stop rule: stop sampling when the best score so far beats a cost-set bar.

source: Shaikh (2026) Knowing when to ask for help: Bayesian self-escalation in hierarchical LLM agents, arXiv 2608.24087
finding: Casts mid-generation hand-off to a stronger model as optimal stopping over a competence posterior. Proves the optimal policy is a time-varying threshold on the posterior; regret against the oracle is controlled by calibration quality.
numbers: Finite-sample regret bound with n labelled calibration trajectories of length T. Pre-registered test on a Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B to 7B cascade: 2 of 3 predictions confirmed (escalation frontier beats post-hoc routing at equal cost; belief discrimination rises over generation).
quote: better calibration matters more than a smarter router
limits: Single independent author; small models; one pre-registered prediction not confirmed (which one not extracted).
agent_relevance: Stop and escalation bars are only as good as the confidence estimate; the schema notes the model's own stuck signal is weak (r=.17), so use code-measured signals.

source: Ehab, El Gadarri, Farias, Jozefiak and Moallemi (2026) OS-Pruner: pruning chains of thought via optimal stopping, arXiv 2607.11089
finding: Learns whether more chain-of-thought is worth its token cost, as optimal stopping with utility = accuracy minus length cost. Beats fixed-threshold early-exit baselines on the accuracy-length frontier.
numbers: 20 to 60% shorter reasoning with under 2 points accuracy loss. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: length -59.3% on GSM8K (accuracy -0.7 pt), -52.8% on MATH-500 (accuracy +2.7 pt); on AIME only -6.9% at the best operating point. At the largest cost weight (1e-5): length cut 60.6%, 60.8%, 64.4% (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME) but AIME accuracy fell from 48.0 to 33.0.
limits: Needs a trained probe; distilled 7B reasoning models; AIME shows hard tasks need more thinking.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and G12: stopping early helps on easy items and hurts on hard ones, so the bar must depend on difficulty.

source: Wang et al. (2025) OptPO: optimal rollout allocation via Bayesian sequential probability ratio test, arXiv 2512.02882
finding: Treats majority-vote sampling as a sequential probability ratio test: stop drawing rollouts once posterior confidence in a consensus answer passes a bound. Used inside test-time RL (TTRL with GRPO or PPO).
numbers: Error levels (alpha, beta) = (0.05, 0.05). Token savings of 15 to 60% across benchmarks; for example TTRL-PPO tokens 262M down to 144M (45% saving) with accuracy kept or improved. Saving of 43.9% at N=16 against 30.0% at N=32.
limits: Test-time RL setting, math and reasoning sets, label-free rewards from agreement; savings vary by benchmark.
agent_relevance: Supports an agreement-based sequential stop (like two agree and one check passed) that cuts cost without losing accuracy.

source: Di Gioia (2026) Cognitive Friction: decision-theoretic bounded deliberation in tool-using agents, arXiv 2603.30031
finding: HJB optimal-stopping framework for when a tool-using agent should stop querying and act, with a rollout approximation of value of information and a net-utility halting condition. Tested in two simulated environments and one illustrative LLM run.
numbers: Over greedy baselines the full method gains 36 viability points (EMDG) and 33 integrity points (NSTG). Stopping rules alone recover at most 4 points (entropy-stop ablation: viability 56.8 to 60.2; deliberation time 114.5 to 102.6). N=200 Monte Carlo seeds.
quote: purposive stopping baselines confirm that stopping rules alone recover at most 4 viability points
limits: Simulated worlds, accuracy saturated by design; LLM part only illustrative; single author.
agent_relevance: A stop rule alone gave little; most gain came from choosing which source to query. Do not oversell stopping on its own.

source: Peskir and Shiryaev (2006); Chow, Robbins and Siegmund (1971); Weitzman (1978) Optimal search for the best alternative
finding: Standard references named in the pages opened. Weitzman (1978) Pandora's Box gives index-based optimal search with costly boxes and is the base of Kalayci et al. 2025.
numbers: No numbers taken; originals not opened.
limits: Citations only.
agent_relevance: Pandora's Box reservation values are a clean way to rank which operator or attempt to open next.
